article.headline: Financials' Stubborn Lag Sends a Familiar Pre-Correction Signal
article.lede: The S&P 500 closed at 7,444 on May 13, 2026 — a fresh all-time high built on a blowout earnings season and AI-driven optimism — yet the financial sector has conspicuously refused to keep pace, trailing the broader index by more than twelve percentage points over the same stretch. The chart posted by @xtrends, captioned with an inversion of Sir John Templeton's most-quoted aphorism, argues that this divergence has a well-documented history of ending badly. Whether it signals systemic strain or a simple mean-reversion opportunity depends on which piece of history you reach for.
article.body:
The gap is captured in the XLF:$SPX *ratio*, which compares the Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund against the S&P 500. When the ratio falls, financials are underperforming the broad market; the chart records a -12.14% reading as of May 13, 2026. The divergence widened sharply in the first quarter, when XLF declined 9.85% against the S&P 500's shallower 4–5% dip. What makes the signal particularly pointed is that it persisted through the subsequent recovery: the broader index rallied past its prior all-time high and closed at 7,444, but **financial stocks did not participate proportionally**, leaving the ratio gap not just intact but slightly wider.

The headwinds bearing on the sector are concrete. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.50–3.75% even as rate-cut expectations emerged, compressing *net interest margin* — the spread between what banks earn on loans and pay on deposits — and clouding earnings visibility. Mortgage origination volumes sat roughly 68% below pandemic peaks as 30-year fixed rates remained elevated. Proposed legislation — a Credit Card Competition Act, an interest-rate cap on consumer credit, and the finalisation of *Basel III Endgame* capital requirements — added further regulatory drag. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B), together accounting for roughly a quarter of XLF's weight, face the same bind: higher-for-longer rates support existing loan portfolios but constrain new origination and have dampened capital-markets activity.

The bear case embedded in the chart leans on *sector rotation* history. Before the 2007–2008 financial crisis, XLF declined roughly 19.6% in calendar-year 2007 while the S&P 500 posted only modest losses — before both collapsed together in 2008. The logic is intuitive: financials intermediate nearly every economic transaction, so persistent underperformance can signal that credit conditions are quietly tightening beneath an apparently buoyant headline index. The Shiller *CAPE ratio* for the S&P 500 sat around 40.5 by mid-May 2026 — well above its historical average of roughly 17 and approaching the 44.2 peak reached at the height of the 2000 dot-com bubble — adding a valuation dimension to the technical divergence.

The counterargument is that financial sector underperformance may itself be the contrarian signal. XLF's *relative strength index* (RSI) fell below 30 — conventionally “deeply oversold” — during the Q1 rout, and the last time it reached that threshold (during the tariff-driven selloff of April 2025) XLF subsequently rallied more than 20% in under a month. From that vantage, the -12.14% gap is less a warning of systemic fragility than an invitation to rotate into undervalued financials as the AI names that led the recovery grow stretched. Templeton’s original warning — and the tweet’s inversion of it — cuts both ways: if history rhymes, financials either foreshadow a correction in the broader market, or they mean-revert to it.

concepts.definition: A relative performance measure comparing the Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF) — which tracks U.S. banks, insurers, and asset managers — against the S&P 500 index. A falling ratio means financials are underperforming the broad market. Practitioners treat sustained moves in this ratio as a leading indicator of shifting economic momentum, since the financial sector intermediates nearly all credit and capital in the economy.

The spread between the interest income a bank earns on loans and securities and the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings, expressed as a percentage of earning assets. It is the primary driver of bank profitability. NIM compresses when rate-cut expectations reduce future loan yields before deposit costs fall in step, shrinking the profitable gap banks rely on.

The final tranche of post-2008 bank capital reforms agreed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, requiring large banks to hold more high-quality capital against risk-weighted assets. U.S. finalisation was contentious — large banks lobbied hard against the proposed rules — because once implemented, the requirements raise the cost of holding certain assets and can constrain lending capacity and return on equity.

The practice — or emergent market phenomenon — of capital flowing from one industry sector to another as economic conditions or relative valuations shift. In a classic late-cycle rotation, investors move out of growth and technology names into undervalued cyclicals or defensives. Relative performance ratios like XLF:$SPX are a standard tool for spotting when rotation is underway.

The Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings ratio, developed by economist Robert Shiller, divides the S&P 500's price by the inflation-adjusted average of ten years of earnings to smooth out business-cycle noise. A CAPE above 30 is historically associated with elevated valuations; readings above 40 have previously coincided with major market peaks (2000) and periods of subsequently poor long-run returns.

A momentum oscillator, typically calculated over 14 trading days, that measures the speed and magnitude of recent price changes on a scale of 0 to 100. Readings above 70 are conventionally considered overbought; readings below 30 are considered oversold — often a contrarian entry signal. RSI does not predict direction, only the pace of recent movement.

A warning phrase popularised by investor Sir John Templeton, who called it among “the four most dangerous words in investing.” It describes the recurring human tendency to rationalise elevated asset prices by arguing that new circumstances render historical valuation norms obsolete. Economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff later gave the phrase academic weight in their 2009 book of the same title, documenting eight centuries of financial crises driven by precisely this error.

The statistical tendency of an asset’s price or ratio to drift back toward its long-run historical average after a significant departure. In markets it underpins contrarian strategies: a sector that has underperformed sharply may be poised to revert as the forces driving the divergence fade. It cuts directly against momentum strategies, which assume the trend continues.

ticker_jpm.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
ticker_jpm.blurb: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a leading global financial services firm and one of the largest banking institutions in the United States. It operates through four major segments: Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management. The company provides a wide range of services including investment banking, financial transaction processing, asset management, and retail banking. As of 2025, it is the largest bank in the U.S. by assets and a component of the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
ticker_jpm.recent: In the past 30 days, JPMorgan Chase's stock has shown positive momentum, driven by strong quarterly earnings and favorable interest rate expectations. The company reported better-than-expected revenue and profit, benefiting from higher net interest income and robust investment banking fees. Analysts have raised price targets, citing the bank's diversified business model and capital strength.

ticker_brk-b.name: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. Class B
ticker_brk-b.blurb: Berkshire Hathaway is a multinational conglomerate holding company headquartered in Omaha, Nebraska, led for decades by chairman Warren Buffett. It owns a diverse portfolio of wholly-owned subsidiaries spanning insurance (GEICO, General Re), railroads (BNSF), energy (Berkshire Hathaway Energy), manufacturing, retail, and services. The company also holds large equity positions in publicly traded companies including Apple, Bank of America, Coca-Cola, and American Express. BRK.B shares represent 1/1,500th of a BRK.A share and trade at a price accessible to retail investors, making Berkshire one of the largest companies by market capitalization in the world.
